h1: Barbed Wire Fence Installation in Waco, TX
heroSub: Five tight strands, corners that don't lean, and a price you'll see in writing before we drive the first post. Serving McLennan, Bosque, and Falls counties.
introHtml:
When you're pricing barbed wire fence installation in Waco, TX, the numbers that matter are per foot and per mile. A 5-strand barbed wire fence from Brazos Ridge Fence Co. runs $2.50 to $5.50 per linear foot installed, depending on terrain, post type, and how much old fence we're tearing out first. Net wire and field fence for goats, sheep, and horses runs $3.50 to $8 per foot. Those are real installed prices, not teaser rates that grow once we're on your place.

We build fence across McLennan, Bosque, and Falls counties, from small hobby tracts near Lorena to full ranch perimeters out past Crawford. Every job starts with a free written estimate, and we're licensed and insured. If you're comparing options, our ranch fence cost guide breaks down every fence type we build.

sections.heading: 5-Strand Barbed Wire Built for Central Texas Cattle
sections.html:
Five strands is the standard for cattle in this part of Texas, and there's a reason for it. Four strands leave gaps that calves slip through, and six is usually money you don't need to spend on gentle stock. We space strands so the bottom wire discourages calves from rooting under and the top wire sits high enough that a cow won't lean over it.

Installed prices run $2.50 to $5.50 per linear foot. Flat, clean ground with T-posts lands at the low end. Rocky ground, heavy brush clearing, old fence teardown, or pipe line posts push you toward the top. A quarter mile is 1,320 feet, so figure roughly $3,300 to $7,300 for a quarter mile depending on those factors.

Every build includes braced corner and gate assemblies, because a barbed wire fence is only as good as its corners. If a corner leans, the whole stretch goes slack. For the full math on longer runs, see our ranch fence cost page.

sections.heading: Net Wire and Field Fence for Goats, Sheep, and Horses
sections.html:
Barbed wire holds cattle, but goats and sheep treat it like a suggestion. For small stock and horses we install net wire, also called field fence, at $3.50 to $8 per linear foot. The woven mesh stops animals that push, climb, or squeeze, and a single barbed strand on top keeps cattle from mashing it down.

Common setups we build around Waco:

  • Sheep and goat fence: net wire with graduated mesh, tighter at the bottom, usually 39 to 48 inches tall
  • Horse-safe field fence: smaller mesh openings so a hoof can't pass through, with a smooth or barbed top wire
  • Combination fence: net wire plus one or two barbed strands on top for mixed cattle and small-stock pastures

If you're keeping deer out instead of stock in, that's a taller build. Take a look at our game fence installation page for high-fence options.

sections.heading: T-Posts or Pipe Posts: Spacing That Actually Holds
sections.html:
Most of the fence we build uses steel T-posts on the line and pipe at the stress points. On typical Central Texas ground we drive T-posts every 8 to 10 feet. On flat, open ground with good wire tension you can stretch that to 12 feet, and on hills or creek crossings we tighten it up. Post spacing is where cheap fence jobs cut corners, and it's why they sag in three years.

Pipe belongs at corners, gates, and pull points. We set pipe corner and H-brace assemblies in concrete, because those posts carry the tension of the entire stretch. On some ranches we run pipe line posts too, every 20 to 30 feet with wire, for a fence that shrugs off leaning cattle and falling limbs.

Want the heavier build? Our pipe fence page covers all-pipe fencing, and if you're dressing up the front of the place, we build ranch entrance gates to match.

sections.heading: Ag Exemptions and Storm-Damage Repair
sections.html:
A lot of our calls start with an ag valuation. To qualify land for agricultural appraisal in McLennan, Bosque, or Falls county, the appraisal district wants to see the land actually used for agriculture, and for most folks around here that means grazing. You can't graze cattle without a stock-tight perimeter, so a sound 5-strand fence is usually the first real investment in qualifying a property. We're fence builders, not tax advisors, so confirm requirements with your county appraisal district, but we'll build the perimeter that makes a grazing lease possible.

Storms are the other half of this business. Central Texas wind and flood water take out fence every year, and a gap in the wire at midnight means cattle on the road by morning. That's a liability problem, not just a fence problem.

Our emergency line at (254) 555-0184 answers 24/7 for storm damage and cattle-out calls. We'll patch the gap fast to contain your stock, then come back for the permanent repair on a written estimate. We handle emergency calls across the area, from China Spring and Valley Mills down to McGregor and West.

faq.q: How much does barbed wire fence installation cost in Waco, TX?
faq.a: A 5-strand barbed wire fence runs $2.50 to $5.50 per linear foot installed. Clean, flat ground with T-post line posts sits at the low end, while rock, brush clearing, old fence removal, or pipe posts push the price up. We give you the exact number in a free written estimate before any work starts.

faq.q: What does a mile of barbed wire fence cost?
faq.a: A mile is 5,280 feet, so at $2.50 to $5.50 per foot you're looking at roughly $13,000 to $29,000 installed. A quarter mile, which is 1,320 feet, runs about $3,300 to $7,300. Long straight runs on open ground usually price better per foot than short, choppy stretches with lots of corners.

faq.q: How far apart should fence posts be for barbed wire?
faq.a: We drive steel T-posts every 8 to 10 feet on typical ground, and up to 12 feet on flat open stretches with good wire tension. Corners, gates, and pull points get pipe posts set in concrete, since they carry the tension of the whole run. If a fence company quotes you 15-foot spacing, that fence will sag early.

faq.q: Do I need a fence to get an ag exemption on my land?
faq.a: The fence itself doesn't grant the exemption, but grazing does, and you can't graze without a stock-tight perimeter. County appraisal districts in McLennan, Bosque, and Falls counties want to see genuine agricultural use, and a 5-strand perimeter fence that holds cattle is usually step one. Confirm the exact requirements with your appraisal district, and we'll handle the fence.

faq.q: Can you fix storm-damaged fence fast if my cattle are getting out?
faq.a: Yes. Call our 24/7 emergency line at (254) 555-0184 and we'll get out to contain the gap, often the same day. We patch first so your stock stays put, then give you a written estimate for the permanent repair. Downed trees on wire, washed-out water gaps, and flattened corners are the most common calls after Central Texas storms.
